1:
The army came home expecting thanks. Henry has Joab and his troops follow the messengers to grace the king's triumph and take further orders, and find instead a damp on everything, the tears looking to them like displeasure at what they had done. Gill marks the sequence: the report reached Joab on his way to Mahanaim, perhaps from the messengers he had sent, so that he knew before he saw the king. Henry notes how fast it ran, and draws the lesson that people watch what their princes say and do, so that the more eyes are on a man the more need he has to govern his passions. Gill and Clarke describe the reversal from the soldiers' side: they mourned instead of rejoicing, grieving over their own success because the king was so immoderately afflicted for a worthless son and a rebellion that deserved quashing. Four voices describe the entry. Gill has them come in privately, one by one or a few together, rather than marching in companies as conquerors do, not caring to be seen by a king whose displeasure they feared, and Wesley adds the fear of being looked on with an evil eye as men who had a hand in killing a beloved son. Keil and Delitzsch keep the narrator's own comparison, that they stole in like men ashamed after fleeing a battle. Gill has the king refuse to see his generals or thank them, wrapping himself in his mantle after the manner of mourners.

Henry brings two counts against the mourning. The first is that David proclaimed it, when he ought to have been ashamed and would have smothered it had he considered either his reputation for courage, lessened by so mean a submission to an absurd passion, or his standing with the people, injured by discountenancing what was done in zeal for his honour and the public safety. Henry fills in the cry as the thought of a man whose servants have all come home safe while his son is dead in his sin, so that he cannot say he shall go to him. The second is that he prolonged it until the army had come up, when an hour or two's vent would have been excusable; Henry's comparison is Jacob mourning for Joseph, a good son where this was a bad one, with a resolution to go down to the grave mourning and stain a victory with tears. He allows that the people were loth to blame a king whose actions had always pleased them, but says they felt it as a mortification, and that superiors ought not to lay such hardships on inferiors. Clarke takes the lament as a form rather than a fault: the covered face was the custom of mourners, and the repeated name is, as Calmet observes, the ordinary language of grief, for which he quotes a pastoral poem of Virgil's that repeats a dead shepherd's name the same way.

Keil and Delitzsch read the mourning as the root of all that follows. On their account his passionate and sinful sorrow made him forget what he owed to the recovery of his people's affections, so that Joab had to remind him of a duty binding on a king; and it carried him into inconsiderate measures and acts of imprudence and injustice that could not strengthen his throne, however clearly the kindness he later pressed on Barzillai showed a king who wished his subjects well. Their reading of Joab's charge is that the servants' faces were covered with shame by the deceiving of their expectation. They also notice a seam, the fifth verse taking up the thread of the first, with the three between as a parenthesis on the army's mood. Clarke's material here is a synopsis of the whole chapter rather than comment on these verses, bearing on what is coming rather than on the mourning.
5:
Joab's intervention is admired and deplored in the same breath. Gill places it in the palace, the king having moved from the chamber over the gate to his own house, where he kept up the same doleful note as before. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the shaming as a covering with shame through the deceiving of the servants' hope that their king would rejoice in the victory, Wesley as the disappointing of their just hopes of praise and reward, requited with contempt and tacit rebuke. Clarke's estimate is double-edged: the speech is remarkable for the insolence of office and also for good sense and firmness, since any candid reader must allow that David acted imprudently and needed rousing to his duty — yet Joab went far beyond the reverence a servant owes his master, being a good soldier and in every other respect a bad man and a dangerous subject. Ellicott finds the whole character in the scene: a man whose hand was red with the blood of the beloved son, reproaching the father for his grief in the hardest terms, treating the king with thorough insolence and the air of a superior, and counselling him all the while for his own good and the kingdom's like a wise and loyal statesman. Whether David yet knew Joab's part in the death he thinks doubtful. Gill allows that the words were advice rather than command, and explains the liberty taken by the standing of a general in those times, who presumed on his interest in the army. Keil and Delitzsch hold him not merely justified but bound to expostulate, in the king's own interest.

How much of the accusation is true is a second question. Gill grants an appearance of truth greatly exaggerated, since the grief was for an enemy who had rebelled and the neglect fell on friends who had exposed their lives. Wesley says the same, that it is not exactly true, though David's carriage gave the suggestion too much colour, and that such sharpness was needed to wake the king out of his lethargy and preserve him from the mischiefs hanging over him. Keil and Delitzsch render the sentences flatly: he loves those who hate him and hates those who love him, his conduct has declared commanders and soldiers worth nothing, and he would have been content had Absalom lived while every one of them perished. They take the summons as an instruction to speak to the heart of his servants, which is to say in a friendly manner. Ellicott reads the oath narrowly and denies the construction that makes it a threat of revolt: Joab does not appear to have conceived such a design, much less expressed it, and the violence of the language is there to startle a king out of the selfishness of his sorrow.

The yielding is recorded without a word of feeling, and the commentators fill it in. Gill has him rise from the couch he had watered with his tears and leave the house where he had shut himself from all company, for the gate where a crowd would gather. The gate interests two of them: Gill calls it the public place where the inhabitants met on various errands, and Clarke the place where justice was administered. Keil and Delitzsch note that he was obliged to yield in the end, and that the good-will he showed the troops in looks and words has to be supplied from the context, the narrative not describing it. The last clause of the verse they take as a transition rather than a detail, the portion of the people that had followed Absalom having gone home to its tents. Ellicott would translate it adversatively, as a contrast rather than a reason, and adds the usage that governs the whole narrative, in which the name Israel stands for those who had espoused Absalom's cause.
9:
Henry begins with a question the narrative does not raise: why the king waited to be fetched, when he had a victorious army and the rebels were still scattered. His three reasons are all about the manner of the return. David would go back as a prince, with the people's consent rather than as a conqueror forcing his way, restoring their liberties instead of encroaching on them. He would go back in safety, knowing before he stirred that the country was well affected. And he would go back in honour, not at the head of his forces but in the arms of his subjects — for Henry's maxim is that a prince with wisdom and goodness enough to be his people's darling cuts a better figure than one with strength enough to be their terror. On this reading the delay is policy, not sloth, and the invitation had to come from the tribes first.

What the tribes were quarrelling about is described four ways and amounts to one thing. Gill has every tribe but Judah reproving its neighbours both for siding with Absalom and for the coldness and backwardness that had left the king unfetched. Keil and Delitzsch, noting that the rebellion was wholly crushed once Absalom was dead and his followers gone home, read the disputing as a casting of reproaches and trace the movement to the consciousness of having wronged the king. Wesley has them quarrelling over who had been the authors and who the abettors of a shameful rebellion, and talking over David's merits in private and in public, which he takes for a memory God revived now that he was reconciled to David. Ellicott puts it as a collapse of infatuation: with the rising broken the people began to remember what they owed the king, and a general disposition to return to their allegiance appeared, though without organisation or leadership. Henry sets out the two arguments actually urged, that a benefactor who had fought their battles and subdued their enemies should not be left in banishment, and that the man they had preferred had now disappointed them, they having been foolishly sick of the cedar and chosen the branch to reign over them. His shrewder suggestion is that the strife may not have been over whether to bring the king back, which all agreed on, but over whose fault it was that nobody had — the people blaming the elders, the elders the people, each tribe the next. Mutual encouragement to a good work is laudable, Henry adds, and mutual accusation over its neglect is not, since in such cases every side generally has a share of the blame.

The claim to have anointed Absalom is the verse's difficulty. Gill will allow it either as something actually done by Absalom's party or as the effect of proclaiming and appointing him king. Ellicott presses harder: no other passage mentions an anointing, the high priests would certainly not have performed it, so either some prophet did it or the words are a form of speech borrowed from the custom and mean no more than that they had appointed him. On the reproach that follows, Wesley has the people addressing the elders, as a comparison with the next verse shows, and testifying by their forwardness that they repented of the whole undertaking. Ellicott reads the hesitation as a want of organisation with a dangerous tendency in it, and the moment as the one where David's political skill shows itself again. Both he and Keil and Delitzsch notice the same textual oddity, the clause about the speech of all Israel reaching the king: Keil and Delitzsch treat it as a circumstantial clause dropped into the middle of David's own words to explain the appeal, and observe that the Greek and some Latin copies carry it twice over, while Ellicott calls the Greek placement of it here quite unnecessary.
11:
Why Judah of all tribes had to be courted is the first thing explained. Gill has the two priests at Jerusalem and in the king's interest, approached perhaps through their own sons. Clarke reads the message as a calculated risk, since David dared not fall out with a tribe that held Jerusalem, had joined the rebellion and was doubtless ashamed of it; so he takes no notice of the infidelity and places confidence in them instead, that their confidence in him might be drawn out in return. Ellicott gives the harder version of the same facts: Judah had shown especial ingratitude, had been the cradle and centre of the rising, and probably still had a garrison of Absalom's soldiers in the capital, so that its men might reasonably doubt their reception while their own military organisation stood in the way. Wesley puts it shortest: the abettors of the rebellion despaired of pardon and were backward about the restoration, and he reads the king's house as Mahanaim, where the household then was. Ellicott adds a textual suspicion, that the closing words of the verse may be an accidental repetition of the clause before them.

The lever David uses is kinship, and the commentators weigh how much it was worth. Gill takes the appeal to mean that a king will deal gently with men of his own tribe, as with parts of his own body, rather than press them for their share in the conspiracy as they feared he would. Ellicott notes that the word is singular, bone rather than bones, and that while Judah was of course nearer to David in blood than any other tribe, what would actually move them was the king's open acknowledgement of the tie. The same form of words is then used on the rebel general, and Gill explains his position: the man who had led Absalom's army into the field against the king's troops might well think his own case desperate whoever else was pardoned. Ellicott adds that Amasa was David's nephew as Joab was, though his mother may have been only a half-sister to the king.

The offer of the command is where the readings part. Ellicott calls it bold but rash and unjust, since a traitor-general should have been punished rather than rewarded, had given no evidence of loyalty and no proof he would prove trustworthy, and his promotion was certain to provoke Joab; he explains it by a king long restless under Joab's overbearing influence and, after the killing of Absalom, determined to be rid of him, who seized the chance to win over what was left of the rebel army. Keil and Delitzsch divide the message in two, holding it wise to approach his own tribe, lest Judah, where the rising began, should look dissatisfied with his victory and feed the jealousy between itself and the rest, but both unwise and unjust to bind himself by oath to the rebels' commander. Wesley sees no injustice at all, only a king gladly taking the opportunity of a man with greater interest than Joab, both to chastise the murderer of Absalom and to rescue himself from the bondage Joab had held him in. Clarke judges the whole policy well calculated, and states the principle: show distrust where you have some reason to suspect and you increase a man's caution and distrust, place as much confidence in him as you safely can and his confidence follows. On who bowed the heart of Judah, Gill reports that the Jewish commentators generally understand it of Amasa working on his tribesmen, but prefers to understand it of David, and Keil and Delitzsch agree that the subject is David and neither Amasa nor Zadok. Gill makes the same point at the end: the king could have returned without leave as their lawful and victorious sovereign, with power to punish, and chose instead to gain their hearts.
15:
The crossing is given a weight of its own. Gill measures the march from Mahanaim at twenty-eight miles on Bunting's count, and Ellicott sets the king on the eastern side of the ford near Jericho, Judah's representatives at Gilgal opposite. Keil and Delitzsch say what Judah came for: to form an escort at the passage. Henry thinks Jordan had perhaps never been crossed with so much solemnity since Israel passed it under Joshua, and notices that the king who had remembered God from that land in his flight now found it graced with the glories of his return. The boat sent for the household divides them. Gill explains it was for wives and children who could not ford the stream, reports the opinion that it was a bridge of boats, and adds Abarbinel's suggestion of men carrying the women and children over on their shoulders one by one. Clarke observes that this is the first mention of such a thing, and some take it for a bridge or raft. Henry has the soldiers shift for themselves and a boat sent on purpose for the family; Keil and Delitzsch have the men wade a ford while the boat crossed to put itself at the king's sole disposal.

Two men met him at the bank, and Henry's point is that both had wronged him in the flight. The one had wronged him with a fair tongue, obtaining a grant of his master's estate by accusation and imposing on the king's credulity until he dealt unkindly by the son of his own friend; he comes now with a train of sons and servants to secure favour before his master can undeceive the king. Wesley reads the same calculation: a man conscious of an abuse he knew would come to light, hoping to sweeten the king's temper by being early. The other had wronged him with a foul tongue, and Henry is blunt about the change of posture: had the king been beaten this man would have gone on trampling and boasting, but seeing him come home to his throne he found it his interest to make peace. Ellicott agrees on the motive and values the man anyway, since he was of real influence and his accession worth much at that juncture, though a time-server, disloyal at heart, who had recognised the winning cause. On the thousand Benjamites, Clarke infers a powerful chieftain, Gill offers three possibilities — soldiers under his command, tenants who showed his standing, or neighbours of figure prevailed on to come as intercessors — and Wesley takes them for a display of interest and a body of witnesses, who would see in his case what the rest might expect.

Henry sets out three things done to recommend the submission. He came in good company, with the men of Judah, as though of their party; he brought his thousand, the more obliging in that of all the tribes only these and Judah came out to pay the king this respect; and he lost no time, on the principle of agreeing with an adversary quickly. His falling down was public, before the king's servants, the men of Judah and his own thousand, since as Henry says a public offence requires a public submission. Two are careful about the geography of the moment. Ellicott points out that the phrase for going over before the king means before his face, that is, to meet him, and pictures men so eager to prove a doubtful allegiance that they dashed through the ford to the eastern bank. Keil and Delitzsch argue that the prostration came as David was about to cross rather than after the man had crossed, since the second sense would make the remark superfluous and the construction can hardly bear a pluperfect; Ellicott renders it the same way and notes that the king's own crossing is not described until the paragraph about Barzillai.
19:
The plea is read as a real confession by the two who comment on its wording. Gill explains the request not to impute iniquity as a request not to be dealt with according to the desert of the thing, since non-imputation of sin amounts in effect to its pardon. On the confession that follows he is willing to grant feeling as well as words: the man was sensible of his sin and sorry for it, acknowledged it publicly before his own followers and the king's servants, and offered his early submission as a token of sincere repentance and an earnest of future fidelity. Clarke is cooler but comes to the same practical conclusion, that an avowal was all the man could offer, that only his later conduct could prove it genuine, and that on such an admission David could hardly refuse him his life.

The claim to be first of the house of Joseph needs explaining, since the speaker was a Benjamite. Ellicott takes the name of the most prominent tribe to stand for all the tribes outside Judah, a usage well attested later, and then meets an argument built on it, that so late a usage would date the book late. His answer is that it turns up in psalms whose date it would be rash to fix, in the reign of Solomon, and probably very early in the book of Judges, so that nothing prevents its having been used from the time when a distinction between Judah and the rest first appeared, soon after the conquest of Canaan. Wesley reaches the same identification by a different route, through the division of the firstborn's rights between Judah and Joseph, and adds the detail that Benjamin, later attached to Judah, marched in the wilderness under the standard of Joseph, which is why one psalm names Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh together.

The demand for execution is answered with a word the commentators find remarkable. Gill identifies the man who made it as the same who had offered to take the railer's head off at the time of the cursing, and Ellicott notes that the term David throws back at him is, in the original, Satan. Wesley expands the reply at length: the sons of Zeruiah were pressing him to what was unfit and against his own interest, when his business was to appease the people rather than give fresh offence by severity, which would only make others suspect he was watching his chance at them; and the man whose kingdom had been as good as lost and was now restored, whose own sin God had just forgiven, would neither show himself revengeful nor sully the public joy of such a day. Gill limits the pardon carefully to death by the king's own hand or order. Ellicott reads the whole affair politically and follows it to its end: the treason was real, the confession and the help toward the restoration were real too, the pardon was therefore fair, but confirming it by oath was rash, since it left the king unable to punish any later disloyalty. From the man's character, and from the way Solomon afterwards addressed him, Ellicott concludes he stayed a traitor at heart; David saw it, and being bound by his own oath pointed the case out to his son, who settled it by a compact the man willingly accepted, that he should forfeit his life if he left Jerusalem, where he could be watched. He broke the condition within a few years and was executed. David, on this account, kept a rash oath to the letter and no further.
24:
The neglected body is treated as the first piece of evidence. Keil and Delitzsch list the three signs — feet unwashed, beard untrimmed, clothes unwashed, from the flight to the peaceful return — and class them as marks of deep mourning. Wesley explains why each told: washing the feet was usual and refreshing in that climate, so its neglect suited a mourner, and the beard was left long and disorderly as men in a forlorn state wore it — all of it proving him an obstinate mourner and disproving what had been said against him. Clarke draws the same conclusion in a sentence, that the man had given the fullest proof of his attachment and amply refuted his servant's calumny. Henry makes the return a day of bringing things to remembrance, and reads the long squalor as the posture of a man abandoned to grief for the king's affliction and the kingdom's misery, with the moral that public calamity calls for abridging our enjoyments of sense. Two smaller points: Ellicott notes that the word for beard here covers only the moustache, and Gill, remarking that a grandson may be called a son, cites versions making him Saul's son's son or Jonathan's son.

Where he came from, and who came to meet whom, is genuinely disputed. Ellicott prefers the obvious sense, a man coming down from the high ground of Jerusalem to the king in the Jordan valley, which requires the next verse to say that Jerusalem, its inhabitants with him among them, came out to the king. He reports the alternative fairly: some keep that verse as it stands and suppose he had sheltered during the rebellion on his ancestral estate near Gibeah and came from there to Jerusalem; the mourning proves loyalty on either account. Keil and Delitzsch argue the same construction and reject three proposals: an emendation making the phrase mean from Jerusalem, superfluous because the verb of descent already carries it; a change of the verb's form on the ground that a city is feminine, answered by the masculine construction of towns when the inhabitants are meant; and the Greek rendering that makes the lame man the one arriving, which conflicts with the verb and with an earlier verse. Gill leaves the question open, and Wesley supposes he had stayed near Jerusalem because he could not travel as others did.

The king's question suggests he was already half persuaded. Ellicott thinks it so gentle and kindly that the man's appearance had made its impression at once and raised a doubt about the story David had believed. The answer turns on an ass. Gill has the servant going off with the beast he was ordered to saddle, and another besides; Ellicott draws the strands together, since the two asses laden with provisions brought to the king during the flight turn out to have been the ones prepared for the master, left helpless in his lameness when they were taken. Keil and Delitzsch defend the text: if the verb means he had the ass saddled by a servant rather than saddled it himself, the sense is plain and nothing needs altering, since a thing is commonly said to be done by a man who did not do it with his own hands; the Greek and Latin versions, which have him telling the servant to saddle, catch the sense without being true to the words. Henry sets out two injuries from one man who should have been a friend: kept from following the king by the theft of his transport, which took base advantage of his lameness, and then slandered as aiming at the throne. His comment on the acknowledgement that follows is that a man whose whole house had lain at the king's mercy and been set at his table has thereby answered the charge, since nobody so easily placed would be fool enough to aim higher.
27:
The slander is specified, and so is the compliment that follows it. Gill states the charge: the lame man had stayed in the capital with an eye to the throne, hoping the quarrel between father and son would end in restoring the crown to his own family — a calumny with no foundation at all. Keil and Delitzsch argue that he did not infer the slander from the king's tone but had known of it long before, since the servant would hardly have waited to enforce the royal grant of his master's lands, and the enforcement itself would have told him what was said. On the comparison to an angel they are plain, taking it to mean the king sees everything exactly as it is, and Wesley narrows that to the faculty wanted here, telling a true report from a calumny. Clarke expands it into the speech it implies: a case stated plainly and without guile to a man too wise not to see through the motives of both master and servant, with no appeal entered and whatever he decides accepted.

The phrase about dead men draws out the family's real position. Gill weighs two senses. Taken strictly it means men worthy of death, which he grounds not in Saul's old persecution, for which the family did not deserve to suffer, but in another son's attempt on the kingdom, which might be reckoned treason and tainted the house; taken loosely it means only that their lives lay at the king's mercy, and that had he dealt with them as princes commonly dealt with their predecessors' families, death is what they would have had. Wesley reads it the second way, a man before a tribunal where not his estate only but his life had been in the king's power, had the king used the rigour earthly kings use toward the children of predecessors and enemies. Both take the renunciation the same way, that a man so treated has no further claim to press, Wesley specifying what is given up as the vindication of his honour and the restitution of his property. Keil and Delitzsch keep the contrast the speech turns on, a house that might have been put to death and a man set among the king's own companions at table.

The ruling is where Clarke and Ellicott part company. Clarke reconstructs the history to defend it: the estate was granted at first to the grandson, with the servant and his household working it and paying half the produce to their lord; the false report got the whole transferred to the servant; and the king, seeing he had acted too hastily, restores the original arrangement and annuls his own gift. He then asks why the traitor was left anything, and answers that he belonged to Saul's household, which the king wished to treat kindly, and had supplied him with necessaries in his worst distress, so was kept in his old office by way of payment — though the compensation, Clarke adds, was too large for the service when all is weighed. Wesley describes the same settlement, the servant and his sons working the land and keeping their support out of it while the remaining profits went to the owner. Ellicott will have none of it. The hasty transfer was unjust and should at least have been reversed, with punishment for the slanderer besides; what the king does instead he calls a halfway compromise, weak and unjust, explained either by a lingering doubt about the facts or, more likely, by an unwillingness to offend a useful man. What settles the facts for him is the long mourning, the servant's silence, and the man's lameness. Gill reads the reply about taking all as contentment that the last grant should stand, and catalogues what the king refused to hear more of — the old injuries, the favours received, and the question of the land.
31:
The old man is introduced by what he had done. Gill brings him down from Rogelim, the place where he lived, to the river. Henry adds the standing: a noble seat not far from Mahanaim, and of all the gentry of that country the kindest to the king in his distress, who would likely have suffered for his loyalty had the rebellion succeeded and shall now be no loser by it. On the provisions Henry is warm. A large estate had been given him and he had a large heart to use it with, which Henry says is all a large estate is good for, since reduced greatness obliges us to generosity and oppressed goodness to piety. Keil and Delitzsch put it plainly: the supplies came during the stay at Mahanaim, from a man literally great, that is, very wealthy. Clarke reads back from it: a man who gave such help when the king's case was all but desperate cannot have his congratulations suspected, and the offer was both noble and liberal, wishing at once to compensate such a man and keep such a friend at hand. Henry also notices that he did not stop at the bank but crossed the river too, as proof that he was not weary of a guest who had been so great a charge to him.

Ellicott catches something the translation hides. The word used of the provisioning at Mahanaim is the one the king uses next for feeding his benefactor at Jerusalem — rendered elsewhere nourish and sustain — so the offer returns the service in kind, multiplied manifold. The age gets attention too. Gill reckons fourscore years as ten beyond the common term of man's life, a very great age then and since, and notices that the two were at cross purposes about the destination: the old man had come to see the king over Jordan, the king meant to carry him on to Jerusalem. Henry gives the invitation two motives: the pleasure of his company and the benefit of his counsel, for we may suppose him wise and good as well as rich, since it is what a man is rather than what he has that makes him great; and the chance to repay the kindness, with a promise of faring as sumptuously as the king himself in the royal and holy city. Henry commends the king for treating the kindness as a favour to be rewarded and not a debt owed by a subject, being none of those arbitrary princes who reckon whatever their subjects have to be theirs when they please.

The refusal begins with a question about time. Keil and Delitzsch render it as asking how many days of his years are left, that he should go up to Jerusalem at all. Henry hears a man lessening his own service and magnifying the return offered for it, on the principle that a master does not thank the servant who has only done his duty, and who thought himself honoured enough in being of any use to the king. The rest of the reasoning Henry sets out as unfitness of two kinds. There is unfitness for the business of a court: what could he do there, in the council, the camp, the treasury or the courts of justice, and shall a man think of going into business when he is going out of the world? And there is unfitness for a court's pleasures, thrown away on one who could relish them so little — strength at fourscore being labour and sorrow, these the years of which men say they have no pleasure in them, dainties insipid when desire fails, and songs reaching an aged ear much as they reach a heavy heart. His application: the old should learn here to be dead to the delights of sense, letting grace second nature and making a virtue of necessity.
35:
The catalogue of infirmities is taken literally. Gill will not press the number as an exact birthday, only as an age the man had about reached, and probably had. Clarke finds two things in the verse at once, an affecting description of old age and an accurate account of how an Eastern court lived: an ear grown dull, a palate with no relish left, so that the speaker was not merely old but infirm. On the singers he is expansive. Vocal music was a principal part of court entertainment, male and female singers being a necessary appendage to such banquets as they still are in Eastern courts, and a king who was himself a sublime poet, styled the sweet singer of Israel, must have kept his court well supplied with voices and instruments, and probably with poets and poetesses too, since he is unlikely to have been the only poet of his time, however much the best. Wesley compresses the whole refusal into its reason, that dulled senses cannot relish a court's pleasures and that age had made the man useless and burdensome, and so unfit for such a life.

What he asks for instead is small and exactly bounded. Gill reads the request twice over as going a little way beyond the river and then turning back to his own city, having seen the king that far on his journey. The son offered in his place is not named as a son here, and both commentators who notice it reason from elsewhere. Clarke infers it from the dying charge to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai, and adds that the habitation of Chimham near Bethlehem, mentioned long afterwards, was probably a portion of the king's own paternal estate made over to him. Ellicott draws the same inference from the same charge, observing carefully that the narrative here allows it but does not state it. Gill notes only that the king accepted the son in the father's room.

The parting is told shortly, and one word of it is disputed. Gill has all the people who were with the king cross over, and Ellicott adds the usage: as the name of Israel has stood throughout for the rebel party, so the people stands for those who stayed loyal. On the kiss there is no disagreement — Clarke takes it for the token of friendship and farewell — but on what followed there is. Clarke makes the blessing the king's, a prayer for his benefactor's prosperity and perhaps a prophetical benediction; Keil and Delitzsch make the kiss the king's leave-taking and the blessing the old man's, before he turned and went home. They add that the escort went no further than the river, so that the whole conversation was probably held in crossing it.
40:
Who was present at the halt is the fact the quarrel turns on. Gill gives the distance to Gilgal as fifty furlongs on Josephus's reckoning, something over six miles. Keil and Delitzsch place it in the plain of the Jordan, note that the son's name appears in a modified form here, prefer the easier of two readings for the clause about the escort, and explain the half of Israel as the thousand Benjamites who came with the pardoned railer together with other Israelites living nearby. Ellicott accounts for the imbalance by the king's own management: Judah, deeply moved by his measures and his words, had come in generally, while the other tribes, who had actually been the first to talk of returning to their allegiance, either had not heard of the crossing or had no time to reach it, so that only the Benjamite contingent, their neighbours, and the tribes east of the river made up the number. Wesley reads the same half as a measure of guilt and encouragement: the other tribes were no less guilty of the rebellion than Judah, but had been sent no such gracious message, and so came in slowly and by halves — which he marks as the occasion both of this contention and of the sedition that follows it.

Henry sets the scene as a ceremony missed. The king had crossed attended only by the men of Judah, and by the time the elders and great men of the other tribes arrived at the first stage beyond the river, the solemnity of the entrance was over and they had come too late for it. That put them out of humour, and the quarrel it bred Henry calls a damp on the joy of the day and the beginning of further mischief. Their complaint, as he states it, was that the thing had been done without notice that would have let them join; and the sting of it was the reflection it carried, as though they were less well affected to the restoration than Judah — when the king himself knew they had spoken of fetching him back before Judah thought of it — and as though Judah meant to monopolise the royal favour and be taken for his only friends. Henry's verdict on the whole business is that this is what comes of pride and jealousy.

The wording of the charge is weighed by the others. Keil and Delitzsch have the representatives meet the king at Gilgal and, annoyed at being anticipated, ask why their brethren had stolen him away, that is, fetched him secretly without a word to them; and they identify the men brought over with him as the faithful adherents who had fled from Jerusalem at the start. Wesley glosses each phrase: those who came were such as were present, the stealing was a hasty conveyance over the river that did not wait for their concurrence, and the men were the king's officers, guards and soldiers — the aggravation being that Judah had taken the whole establishment across without asking anyone's advice. Gill makes the party a large one, the principal men of the tribes that had not crossed, meeting the king on the road. Ellicott treats the halt as natural and the wrath as old. Jealousy between Judah and the ten tribes had always existed, with Ephraim the most sensitive of them; Saul's successful wars held it in check; it broke out into national separation when he died; David partly healed it after seven and a half years and Solomon's administration kept it quiet; and at Solomon's death it broke out with fresh force and divided the nation for good.
42:
Judah's answer rests on two claims, kinship and disinterest. Gill identifies the speakers as the men who had actually gone down to fetch the king and were now being taken to task for it. Keil and Delitzsch render the reply as a plea that the king stands near to them, since he belonged to their tribe, followed by a denial of having eaten from the king — of having drawn any advantage from the relationship, as the Benjamites once did from Saul — and they note that the second verb is an infinitive absolute with an irregular termination, literally asking whether any taking has been taken for them. Clarke gives the same sense without the grammar: nothing was done for their own advantage, nothing was gained, and loyal attachment was the whole motive. Wesley draws the kinship tighter, a king of their own tribe owing them more respect and expecting more from them, and turns the denial into a reproach, since they had only discharged their duty with all expedition, which the others should have done instead of coming in by halves. Ellicott hears a taunt inside the disclaimer, aimed at the Benjamites and the partiality Saul had shown them.

The counter-claim is arithmetical, and the arithmetic needs explaining. Keil and Delitzsch set ten tribes against one, the Levites not coming into the reckoning, and point out that a king sprung from Judah was king of the whole nation, so that ten tribes held the larger share; the reproach of being despised refers to Judah's taking no notice of them in the fetching, and the last clause asks whether their word had not been first for bringing the king back. Wesley notices that ten understates the count, which was strictly eleven, and offers two explanations, either that Joseph was reckoned as one tribe for Ephraim and Manasseh together, or that Simeon, whose lot lay inside Judah, was counted with Judah in this action. His gloss on the claim of greater right is the sharpest thing in the exchange: the ten urge both that they are the far greatest part of the king's subjects and that Judah had been the first beginner and most zealous promoter of the rebellion. Clarke states the proportion baldly, ten tribes to one, and infers the right to have been consulted. Ellicott notes that the Greek adds a claim of being the firstborn, which he calls an unnecessary gloss and untrue of Benjamin in particular, a tribe probably prominent in the argument.

On the closing remark about fierceness the commentators go opposite ways. Clarke takes the fiercer words as the weightier ones, on the ground that the side which spoke them had more reason behind it. Wesley reads the same clause as a failure of temper: instead of mollifying their brethren with gentle words they answered with greater fierceness, and the quarrel grew hot enough that the king did not dare to interpose. Keil and Delitzsch say only that the answer annoyed the other side, and leave the comparison where the narrator put it. Clarke then takes the dispute as a text for a long reflection on government, in which rivalry between provinces in attachment to a prince is a happy thing that civil wars are unlikely to grow out of, where he deserves it by being pastor and father to his people; a prince who does not try to deserve such confidence is criminal, and so is a people that will not repay the effort; and since a king in a government that is not despotic acts by his ministers' counsel, the maxim that he can do no wrong holds while he does so, with God remaining the only ruler of princes. Ellicott's verdict is quieter, that a quarrel in which each side can plead its disinterest is a remarkable testimony to the fairness of this king's government between the tribes.
